newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon holds delayed local elections on Sunday. [CORRECTED 08:40 GMT 20/10]
newsitem.headline: Gabon holds delayed local elections on Sunday. [CORRECTED 08:40 GMT 20/10]

text.p: Oil-rich Gabon holds local elections on Sunday in the first test of a 1994 deal between government and opposition to set its democratic transition back on course and defuse sometimes bloody political rivalry.

A total of 12,282 candidates will be standing for election as councillors or mayors in the Central African former French colony's nine provinces. Polls open at 7 a.m. (0600 GMT) and close at 6 p.m. (1700 GMT).

President Omar Bongo's Gabonese Democratic Party and its main opposition rivals were among 700 party and independant lists, National Electoral Commission President Gilbert Ngoulakia told Reuters on Saturday.
Policitians complained that voters were showing little enthusiasm for Sunday's poll.
There was also confusion about the number of people who would be able to vote in the nation of 1.2 million people.

Voter registration ended on October 17 but election officials said computer generation of 400,000 registration and voting cards was behind schedule and some voters would have to fill in forms by hand.
Commission documents suggested that only 51,213 voters had registered to vote in the capital Libreville out of an estimated population of 300,000.

"Many people are leaving town to vote in the country," said Commission logistics commissioner Vincent Mintsa. Candidates were opting to stand in provinicial areas with which they had links and supporters were registering outside of Libreville to vote for them, he added.
Under the 1994 Paris accords the municipal elections should have taken place in September 1995.
Legislative elections are now scheduled for November 17, a date criticised by some opposition figures who say it leaves too little time to organise.
Bongo, vice-president on independence from France in 1960, became president in 1968 on the death of Gabon's first president, Leon Mba, and set up a one-party state.
He began moves towards a multi-party system in 1990 after a rash or strikes and demonstrations by students and workers.
Bongo won a five-year term with just over 51 percent of votes cast in a disputed 1993 poll which triggered opposition protests. Five people died in the unrest.

Further clashes followed in 1994, in part to back demands for pay rises after the devaluation that year of the CFA franc used in much of French-speaking Africa. The official death toll was nine, the opposition put the toll at 38.
The Paris Accords between the government and the opposition later that year were designed to increase transparency in government and were approved in a referendum in July 1995.
Legislative election were planned for early 1996 but delayed. Parliament's mandate ran out in May.
Paul Mba Abessole, a Catholic priest and leader of the main opposition National Movement of Woodcutters, is a candidate in Libreville. Abessole was runner-up to Bongo in the 1993 poll.
Election officials say first results are expected by Monday but final results may take a lot longer to emerge.
